title: Agnes (c. 304)
hook: a girl of about twelve who would not give up her faith; lambs are blessed on her feast

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lawrence the deacon, who showed the officials the poor. Your line was these are the treasures.

Lambs, carried into a church in Rome, and blessed. It happens on the feast of a saint named Agnes, at a church built over the place tradition says she was buried. Their wool is later spun and woven into a pallium, a narrow band the Pope gives to metropolitan archbishops to wear over their vestments. It's a gentle ceremony for a story that isn't gentle at all. Agnes was a girl, killed for refusing to give up her faith.
screen: `LAMBS IN A CHURCH IN ROME.` → `WOOL FOR THE PALLIUM.` → `A GIRL NAMED AGNES.`

segments.voice: One early witness is Ambrose, the bishop of Milan, in his book On Virgins. First, her age. Ambrose says she is said to have been martyred at twelve. He finds it hard to take in: a cruelty that didn't spare even so young an age, and a faith that wasn't stopped by it. Second, the chains. The officials brought out chains, Ambrose says, and they were too big; her hands were too small for them. Too young to be sentenced, he says, and yet ready to win. She stood, prayed, and bowed her head. Third, the name. Augustine, preaching on her feast, noticed it: Agnes in Latin sounds like agna, a lamb, and in Greek it means pure. Artists picture her with a lamb in her arms, and the lambs in Rome are blessed on her day. Fourth, why a lamb. At Mass, just before communion, Catholics sing or say the Agnus Dei, Lamb of God, taking up the words of John the Baptist in the Gospel of John: "Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who taketh away the sin of the world." A lamb is small, it doesn't fight back, and in that Gospel line it's the one who carries the world's sin. Agnes, small, refusing to fight and refusing to give in, became a picture of that Lamb. Her name is read among the martyrs in the Roman Canon, along with Perpetua and Felicity.
screen: `SAID TO HAVE BEEN TWELVE.` · `TOO SMALL FOR THE CHAINS.` · `HER NAME: LAMB, AND PURE.` · `THE LAMB OF GOD.` · then, large: `THE LAMB.`

segments.voice: Choose one young person you know, a child, a teenager, a student, and think about the pressure they live under: from friends, from screens, from grades, from people who want them to be someone they're not. Hold them gently, the way the lambs are carried in Rome; you don't need to fix anything. If you pray, ask God to give them courage and keep them safe; if you don't, wish them strength.
Agnes. A Roman girl, said to have been twelve, who would not give up her faith, and whose name sounds like lamb. Today's word.
Your line: the lamb. From Blandina and Irenaeus in Lyon, through Perpetua and Felicity, Origen and Cyprian, to Lawrence and Agnes: a week of witnesses. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics keep the memorial of Saint Agnes in the Church's calendar; in Rome, lambs are blessed on her feast and their wool is used for the pallia given to metropolitan archbishops, and at every Mass the people say or sing the Lamb of God before communion.

chat.says: Why are lambs blessed on Saint Agnes's day?

She was a shepherd girl who kept the flocks for Rome's churches before she died.

notes: Ambrose, On Virgins 1.2.5–9 paraphrased: 'she is said to have suffered martyrdom at twelve'; cruelty that did not spare her age; chains too large for her hands; too young to be sentenced, ready for victory; she stood, prayed, bowed her neck. Confirm each detail and section number.
Augustine, Sermon 273.6: 'Agnes' in Latin means lamb (agna) and in Greek pure (hagne). The script presents this as Augustine's observation, not as an etymology. Confirm sermon number.

Lamb-blessing custom: lambs blessed on her feast (at Sant'Agnese, and presented to the Pope), wool used for the pallia. The script omits the number of lambs and says 'a church built over the place tradition says she was buried'. Confirm current practice and wording.
Douay-Rheims John 1:29: confirm exact wording ('Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who taketh away the sin of the world.').
Agnes named in the Roman Canon alongside Perpetua and Felicity: confirm.
